name: CoreWeave
short_description: The specialized cloud whose GPU clusters power much of AI training.
why_relevant: Proved specialized AI cloud beats generalists on price and speed.
history: Founded in 2017, CoreWeave began as a cryptocurrency mining operation before its founders Michael Intrator, Brian Venturo and Brannin McBee pivoted to specialized GPU cloud services for AI workloads. It scaled rapidly by deploying purpose-built data centers, signed a landmark multi-billion-dollar deal with Microsoft in 2023, and raised billions across equity and debt. The company went public on the Nasdaq in early 2025, securing its position as a leading AI infrastructure provider.

name: Lambda Labs
short_description: Rentable GPU cloud plus workstation business serving AI developers.
why_relevant: Made 1-rack Tight 4090 capacity accessible to small teams.
history: Lambda was founded by Stephen Balaban in 2012 as an AI-focused startup before pivoting toward GPU infrastructure. The company developed one of the first one-click GPU cluster offerings, making single-rack 4090 capacity accessible to small teams, then expanded its own GPU cloud for AI training. Backed by hundreds of millions in venture funding, Lambda now serves startups and enterprises needing fast, affordable access to high-end GPUs.

name: VAST Data
short_description: Universal data platform that holds AI data without tiering costs.
why_relevant: Deleted the storage hierarchy for GPU-first data centers.
history: Founded in 2016 by Renen Hallak, Jeff Denworth and Alon Horev, VAST Data built its first all-flash, tierless storage platforms and launched commercially in 2019. Its universal storage architecture eliminated traditional storage hierarchies, winning large AI and enterprise customers. The company raised a Series D at a $3.7 billion valuation in 2023 and continues to expand its data platform for GPU-first data centers and large-scale AI workloads.

name: MinIO
short_description: Runs an S3-compatible object store at petabyte scale, open-source.
why_relevant: The default S3 gateway keeping enterprise data on-premises and sovereign.
history: MinIO was founded in 2014 by Anand Babu Periasamy and Garima Kapoor to build high-performance, S3-compatible object storage as open-source software. Its distributed architecture let enterprises store petabytes on commodity hardware, making it a default gateway for on-premises and sovereign data. In 2022 the company reached unicorn status with a $103 million Series B led by Intel Capital, and it continues to lead hybrid-cloud object storage for AI and analytics.

name: Supabase
short_description: Postgres-based open backend with auth, realtime and storage.
why_relevant: Freed app builders from cloud-framework lock-in with open Postgres.
history: Supabase was founded in 2020 by Paul Copplestone and Ant Wilson as an open-source alternative to Firebase built on Postgres, and it launched through Y Combinator's Summer 2020 batch. The platform quickly became popular with developers for its managed database, authentication and realtime APIs. After raising an $80 million Series B in 2022, it has grown into one of the most widely deployed open-source backend platforms, powering hundreds of thousands of projects.

name: Render
short_description: Deploy apps and databases in one click with automatic scaling.
why_relevant: The frictionless deploy surface thousands of startups launch first on.
history: Created by Anurag Goel, Render made its debut at TechCrunch Disrupt's Battlefield in 2019 and grew into a leading independent Platform-as-a-Service. It simplified deployment with automatic scaling, built-in TLS, a global CDN and managed databases, attracting thousands of startups and AI-native companies. Initially bootstrapped and later venture-backed, Render raised a $100 million Series C in early 2026 at a $1.5 billion valuation, cementing its role as a simpler alternative to hyperscaler clouds.

name: Fly.io
short_description: Runs containers close to users across global edge regions.
why_relevant: Turned anyone's Dockerfile into a distributed application.
history: Fly.io was founded in 2017 by Kurt Mackey to make running containers close to users across global edge regions effortless. The platform gained attention as a generic container-as-a-service built around distributed edge zones and became popular for realtime applications and large-scale Mastodon hosting. Supported by modest seed funding and a strong developer community, it remains a favorite playground for teams running distributed, low-latency workloads.

name: Railway
short_description: Deploy anything instantly with infrastructure that just works.
why_relevant: Compressed a month of setup into a single git push.
history: Railway was founded in 2020 by Jake Cooper and Ben Asher and graduated from Y Combinator's Summer 2020 batch. The platform promised instant deployment of anything from a GitHub repository, removing weeks of infrastructure setup. It quickly became a popular modern alternative to older PaaS offerings, raising tens of millions of dollars including a Series B in early 2026. Today Railway serves developers and teams worldwide as an all-in-one intelligent cloud platform.

name: Neon
short_description: Scale-to-zero Postgres with branching for developer workflows.
why_relevant: Branches databases like branches of code, ideal for staging-friendly apps.
history: Neon was founded in 2020 by Nikita Shamgunov, who previously co-founded SingleStore, together with PostgreSQL veteran Heikki Linnakangas. The team built a scale-to-zero serverless Postgres platform, separating compute from storage to support instant branching and developer-friendly workflows. Backed by investors including GV and Khosla Ventures, Neon gained rapid traction among developers and now powers serverless Postgres for a large community of application and SaaS teams.

name: PlanetScale
short_description: Serverless MySQL with git-style branching for schema changes.
why_relevant: Schema change workflows that never lock the table during deploys.
history: PlanetScale was founded in 2018 by the co-creators and maintainers of Vitess, including Sam Lambert, Sugu Sougoumarane and Jiten Vaidya, to offer MySQL at unlimited scale in the cloud. The service popularized git-style branching for schema changes and became widely used by high-growth startups. After raising a $50 million Series C in 2021, PlanetScale expanded into serverless Postgres and continues to serve teams needing scalable, developer-friendly databases.

name: Hasura
short_description: Instant GraphQL APIs over existing Postgres and REST data.
why_relevant: Real-time GraphQL with security built into the data layer.
history: Hasura was founded in 2017 in Bengaluru, India, by Rajoshi Ghosh and Tanmai Gopal. The company open-sourced its GraphQL engine in 2018, letting developers expose Postgres and other databases as secure, realtime GraphQL APIs almost instantly. Following a $25 million Series A in 2020 and additional growth funding, Hasura expanded its cloud offering used by thousands of enterprises and developer teams worldwide.

name: Convex
short_description: Live data + compute backend that syncs state to the frontend.
why_relevant: Makes the whole backend feel like a single reactive function.
history: Convex was founded in 2019 by James Cowling, a former Twitter and Palantir engineer, with the vision of a reactive backend that syncs live data and compute to front-end applications. The startup launched a platform where the whole backend behaves like a single reactive function, earning a $26 million Series A in 2022 led by a16z with General Catalyst. It is now used by web teams building realtime, collaborative applications.

name: Upstash
short_description: Serverless Redis and QStash messaging for the edge.
why_relevant: Pay-per-request databases aligned with where the code actually runs.
history: Upstash was founded in 2020 in Istanbul, Turkey, focused on serverless data infrastructure for edge environments. Its pay-per-request Redis and QStash messaging services became popular with developers building on serverless and edge platforms, where predictable, usage-based pricing matters. The company later added vector storage for AI workloads, and after several venture rounds it continues to be widely adopted across modern cloud and edge applications.

name: Vercel
short_description: Deploys frontend applications and AI builders at the edge.
why_relevant: Standard deployment layer for the modern Next.js application stack.
history: Vercel was founded in 2015 by Guillermo Rauch as Zeit, the company behind the Next.js framework, and rebranded to Vercel in 2020. It pioneered frictionless frontend cloud deployments with global edge rendering, becoming the standard platform for Next.js applications. With over $860 million raised and a valuation near $9.3 billion following its 2025 Series F, Vercel also expanded into AI developer tools and continues to lead the modern frontend stack.

name: Netlify
short_description: Simplest way to deploy static and serverless frontends.
why_relevant: Invented the effortless-deploy flow everyone now takes for granted.
history: Netlify was founded in 2014 by Mathias Biilmann and Christian Bach and popularized the Jamstack movement with simple static and serverless frontend deployments. The platform brought continuous deployment, a global CDN and built-in forms into one workflow, making effortless site publishing mainstream. After raising more than $200 million in venture funding, Netlify remains a leading web platform used by developers, agencies and enterprises worldwide.

name: Samsara
short_description: IoT platform connecting fleets, equipment and facilities to one dashboard.
why_relevant: Public benchmark for connected operations in trucking and logistics.
history: Samsara was founded in 2015 by Sanjit Biswas and John Bicket, the MIT alumni who previously built Meraki and sold it to Cisco. The company provides connected operations technology, combining hardware sensors, AI video and cloud software for fleets and industrial sites. After raising over $700 million and going public on the New York Stock Exchange in December 2021, Samsara has become a leading public benchmark for IoT-driven fleet and physical operations management.

name: Particle
short_description: Full-stack IoT from SIM-connected modules to a device cloud.
why_relevant: The hardware-software bridge that takes an IoT idea to production.
history: Particle was founded in 2013 by Zach Supalla to simplify building connected products. Its Wi-Fi and cellular modules, launched around the Kickstarter-funded Photon board, made device-to-cloud prototyping accessible for makers and businesses alike. The company built a full-stack IoT platform spanning hardware, connectivity and a device cloud, raising venture funding and serving customers worldwide across consumer and industrial IoT products.

name: Tulip Interfaces
short_description: No-code app platform bridging people and machines on the factory floor.
why_relevant: Gives operators paperless, connected workflows without a developer.
history: Tulip Interfaces was founded in 2014 by MIT alumni Natan Linder and Rony Kubat to give factory operators no-code tools for connecting people and machines. The platform lets manufacturers build app-like workflows without software engineers, gaining broad adoption across production, quality and traceability. Backed by investors including NEA and Mitsubishi Electric, which led a $120 million Series D in early 2026, Tulip continues to expand its frontline operations platform globally.

name: Litmus Automation
short_description: Edge-to-cloud orchestration connecting factory devices with analytics.
why_relevant: Middle-lurk homegrown tools between OT and IT safely.
history: Litmus Automation was founded in 2014 to bridge operational technology and IT in manufacturing through edge data orchestration. Built by founder Vatsal Shah, the company introduced an edge platform connecting factory devices to cloud analytics and earned recognition from Gartner in 2018. With tens of millions in funding, Litmus now offers its Edge Data Platform and Edge AI capabilities to manufacturers pursuing Industry 4.0 and Industrial AI.

name: OnLogic
short_description: Performance rugged computers for edge computing in harsh environments.
why_relevant: Purpose-built machines that survive the industrial edge they serve.
history: OnLogic, originally founded as Logic Supply in 2003, has built rugged industrial computers for edge computing in demanding environments for over two decades. Based in South Burlington, Vermont, the company earned a reputation for fanless, performance-optimized systems deployed across factories, vehicles, agriculture and beyond. Rebranded to OnLogic in 2020, it remains privately held and profitable, shipping millions of devices worldwide for IoT, edge AI and embedded workloads.

name: Seeed Studio
short_description: Open-hardware platform powering maker and industrial IoT prototyping.
why_relevant: The friendly Chinese hardware house behind countless IoT MVPs.
history: Seeed Studio was founded in 2008 in Shenzhen, China, by Eric Pan to make open hardware accessible worldwide. Its Grove modular system and maker-friendly boards, later joined by reComputer edge devices and Meshtastic radio boards, powered countless IoT prototypes and products. Growing through a mix of bootstrapping and community support, Seeed Studio remains a leading Chinese open-hardware house serving both makers and industrial IoT developers.

name: Wiliot
short_description: Battery-free stickers that sense and connect billions of products.
why_relevant: Makes every retail item trackable without batteries or charging.
history: Wiliot was founded in 2017 by Alon Yehevkely, Tal Tamir and Yaron Elboim to connect everyday products to the internet using battery-free sensors. Its stamp-sized ambient IoT Pixels harvest energy from radio waves to track location, temperature and movement without batteries or charging. Having raised more than $300 million, including a Series C in 2026, Wiliot works with retailers and enterprises on item-level supply chain visibility at massive scale.

name: Aclima
short_description: Hyperlocal pollution sensor networks mapping air quality street by street.
why_relevant: Turned pollution into a street-level visible dataset for cities.
history: Aclima was founded in 2010 by Davida Herzl to measure and map environmental health, starting with low-cost air-quality sensor networks. Its mobile sensing grid, deployed in vehicles through a long-running partnership with Google, produced street-by-street pollution maps for cities worldwide. Aclima has raised tens of millions in venture funding and now provides hyperlocal air-quality intelligence to governments, communities and companies seeking real-time environmental insight.

name: InfluxData
short_description: Purpose-built time-series database for device and metrics data.
why_relevant: The standard store for the torrent of IoT and ephemeral stats.
history: InfluxData, founded in 2013 by Paul Dix, created the open-source InfluxDB time-series database to handle the torrent of metrics and device data from modern systems. The company built a complete stack for collecting, storing and querying time-series data at scale for IoT and observability use cases. Now on InfluxDB 3, the company has raised more than $100 million and serves thousands of enterprise customers with its purpose-built time-series platform.

name: Timescale
short_description: Adds time-series performance to Postgres with compression on by default.
why_relevant: One database where metrics, events and application data coexist.
history: Timescale was founded in 2015 by Mike Freedman, a Princeton computer science professor, and Ajay Kulkarni to add time-series capabilities to PostgreSQL. The team open-sourced TimescaleDB in 2017, giving developers compression, continuous aggregates and analytical queries inside a familiar Postgres interface. With more than $100 million raised, the company continues to evolve its open-source platform and cloud offerings for analytics workloads.

name: Aeris
short_description: Two decades of carrier-grade IoT coverage and device management.
why_relevant: Fleet-scale connected devices riding single, redundant networks.
history: Aeris Communications, founded in 1992, built one of the earliest dedicated cellular networks for machine-to-machine communication before evolving into a comprehensive IoT connectivity platform. Through two decades of carrier-grade partnerships, the company connected millions of fleet and enterprise devices while expanding into security, device management and connected-vehicle services. Headquartered in Santa Clara, California, Aeris continues to operate globally from offices spanning the United States, Europe and Asia.

name: FogHorn
short_description: Runs AI analytics at the edge, close to industrial sensors.
why_relevant: Kicks the cloud out of real-time industrial analytics decisions.
history: FogHorn was founded in 2015 to bring AI and realtime analytics directly to industrial edge environments. Its lightweight edge engine lets manufacturers analyze sensor and video data on-site instead of sending everything to the cloud, reducing latency and dependence on connectivity. Raising tens of millions across several rounds and earning industry analyst recognition, FogHorn continues to serve energy, manufacturing and automotive customers with edge AI.

name: Ockam
short_description: Secure-by-design messaging that authenticates identities across connected devices.
why_relevant: Zero-trust for the physical world of hundreds of connected things.
history: Ockam was founded by Matthew Gregory to build secure-by-design communication infrastructure for distributed and connected systems. Its open-source toolkit established end-to-end encrypted, mutually authenticated channels for devices, clouds and autonomous agents, and underwent independent security review by Trail of Bits. The startup raised about $17.5 million before winding down operations in 2026, leaving its open-source work available for the community to continue.

name: Fivetran
short_description: Automated connectors that pipe warehouse-ready data from any source.
why_relevant: Made keeping data in sync a subscription instead of a data-engineering war.
history: Fivetran was founded in 2012 by George Fraser to automate the movement of data from hundreds of sources into centralized warehouses. Its fully managed connectors replaced custom data-engineering pipelines with simple, reliable configuration, and the company became one of the most heavily funded data startups. After several large funding rounds, Fivetran serves thousands of enterprises, including many Fortune 500 names, and continues to power analytics pipelines worldwide.

name: Airbyte
short_description: Open-source data movement platform for ELT pipelines.
why_relevant: Open-source alternative that made data movement source-sticky.
history: Airbyte was founded in 2020 by Michel Tricot and John Lafleur to make data movement open-source and source-sticky. The startup built a massive connector library and a strong open-source community, offering ELT pipelines to data teams worldwide. After raising a $150 million Series B in 2022 at a $1.5 billion valuation, Airbyte expanded into AI data infrastructure while maintaining its position as a leading open-source data integration platform.

name: Pulumi
short_description: Infrastructure-as-code in real programming languages, not DSLs.
why_relevant: Let teams refactor cloud deployments with the same tools as their app code.
history: Pulumi was founded in 2017 by Joe Duffy, Eric Rudder, Luke Hoban and Matt Ellis, veterans of Microsoft and Amazon, to bring infrastructure as code to real programming languages. Its SDKs let developers define cloud infrastructure beside application code, supporting platforms from AWS to Azure to Kubernetes. Backed by more than $100 million in funding, Pulumi continues to help teams manage modern cloud infrastructure with general-purpose languages.
